items.title: Alex Bigard Interview, 1960-04-30
items.q: I know he played with King Oliver... Did you ever hear Oliver play? Oh, yeah, King Oliver. How did he work when you heard him?

ctx.x: They had Walter Deku on piano. Emile Biggoin on violin. And they had Bill Matthews was playing drum.

And they had Joe Howard playing trumpet. Was there a clarinet did you mention? Yes. No. No. Who was the clarinet? Who was the clarinet? Was there a clarinet did you mention? The clarinet player was uh, The clarinet player was uh, Louis Nelson. Biggoin. Oh yeah. Oh yeah. Can you tell us anything about your, anything else about your uncle? Uh, when did he die about? I don't even know. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No.…

items.title: Alex Bigard Interview, 1960-04-30
items.q: And he worked with King Arthur. Mm-hmm. Dead Green, King Arthur. That's the most band that I know he worked with.

ctx.x: They make them themselves? No, no. They bought them, huh? Yeah. They bought them. Now, what do you call jazz music? How would you demonstrate jazz tempo?

That's in order of speaking about it just a while ago. Fast. Yeah. Do you know when that word began being used around here in connection with the bands, when they started calling them jazz bands? About what year? Was it before the war, after the First World War? When was it, do you know? I think it was after the First World War. I think it was after the First World War. Yeah, after the First World War. Because that, before then, it left a dish around here. Well, to change the subject again, I'd like to get back…
You and Barney? No. You haven't played together in a while.

items.title: Alex Bigard Interview, 1960-04-30
items.q: Did he sound anything like Joe Oliver on the blues, would you say? ... Yeah, yeah. He was good.

ctx.x: Was there anything that made the Chris Kelly band stand out so on the blues? What made you so good on the blues?

Well, we had a blues down there used to call it Keller's Love. And he was the only man that could play the Keller's Love. I mean, to suit the people, the puck. Because he used to use that wah-wah on his trumpet. And he used to say he was talking. Oh yeah. Did he use his hand or a plunger, a rubber plunger? A plunger. Rubber plunger. He was a good blues man. Did he sound anything like Joe Oliver on the blues, would you say? Did Oliver use much of that newt work too? Yeah, yeah. He was good. He was the blues king…
Well, you wouldn't say that he played a lot of fast notes or anything like that? Or did he mix it up? Well, he'd mix it up. He could make fast drums or slow stuff. Yeah. Whatever suited, I guess.
